models.summary: A modified Volterra system for the carbon held by a forest and by the wood cut from it. Trees are split into four age stages of about ten to fifteen years: juvenile 27.0 percent, mid-age 25.6, near-mature 24.3, and mature 23.1. The over-ripe stage, about 0.01 percent, is dropped. Stages A and B are never cut, because the stock is small. Stage C is cut moderately and stage D heavily. Saplings reach maturity at a retention of 85 percent, so the mortality at a stage is about 5 percent. Growth and mortality are borrowed from Ameray and coauthors in 2021 and pinned to Prince Albert, Oak Ridge, and Manaus. Ninety percent of a tree becomes wood, and the products lose about ten percent of their carbon a stage. The initial area is the natural distribution and the wood products start with no stored carbon. SciPy integrates the system. On 100 square kilometers of northern-China larch, with a carbon fixation of 25 tonnes per square kilometer from the CO2FIX measurement, moderate cutting (0.3 of the near-mature trees and all of the mature) holds 1360.3 kilotons, no cutting holds 1242.7, and heavy cutting (0.6 and all) holds 1123.6. The store rises up to a 25 percent cut, holds from 30 to 50, and falls past 55. The best cut of near-mature trees is about 37.48 percent.

models.summary: Six values of a forest, summed and maximized by simulated annealing. Output value is the timber sold. Carbon-tax transfer prices the carbon the stand holds. Tourism uses a security factor, a scenic rating, and a reception capacity. Ecological value is taken as already accounted in the literature. Biomass uses an IPCC expansion factor, a carbon transfer of 0.5, and a root-to-stem ratio of 0.42. Other value covers science and a bequest, tied to the age mix. The total is their sum. Biomass and ecology rank first, output and tourism second, and the tax and the rest last, though the worked case weights them equally. The carbon price is weighted to 51.2 dollars a tonne and checked against a reported 50. The world carbon tax averages 60 dollars and the trading price averages 2. Annealing cools by 0.85 and stops below 10 to the minus 30. On northern-China larch, with a stage of ten to fifteen years, the total falls between 27283 and 40924.5 dollars per square kilometer per year.

models.summary: An inverse map from the best total value back to the cut of near-mature trees, then four strategies tried on four climates. The carbon-tax value at the equilibrium is inverted, and the result is divided by 100 because the plan was simulated on 100 square kilometers. Biomass, output, tourism, and the other value are held fixed in the short run. The four strategies are general, soft, natural, and excessive cutting. The four climates are tropical, temperate and subtropical, boreal, and polar or highland. Wood output above 500 is normal and the cut stays, between 100 and 500 the cut falls, and below 100 the cut stops. The tropics take the general cut, the temperate zone the soft cut, and the boreal zone only the natural one. Polar forests can bear no logging strategy. Reserves such as Ratanakiri, Parsar, and Jiufeng rest, so their cut is essentially zero. For a subtropical forest in southern China, 80 percent of the mature trees are cut and 20 percent kept, and the near-mature cut sits between 41.5 and 55 percent as the carbon price runs from 2 to 60 dollars. Over a century, 100 square kilometers take up 442.2 to 820.8 kilotons, a net gain of 68 to 88.

models.summary: An evolutionary game between forest managers and local residents over the harvest. Managers harvest with probability alpha or rest with probability one minus alpha. Residents support with probability beta or oppose. A manager who cuts gets the carbon value and the timber, and may lose the carbon-tax transfer when the public objects. A manager who rests gets only the tax. The two expectations are written out and left blank on the page. MATLAB integrates the game. Even a manager who prefers restoration eight to two, and the indifferent case of one half, converge on the moderate cut. The new policy lengthens the cycle by ten years. In all six simulated forest types the new policy meets the old one and then passes it.
